## Summary

During the Contra war and the US trade embargo, the Sandinista government financed defence and subsidies with the central bank. Hyperinflation lasted almost five years (H&K: **June 1986 – March 1991**), one of the longest on record. The worst month came at the very end: **261 % in March 1991, prices doubling every 16.4 days** (H&K). A 1988 reform cut three zeros; within two years notes were overprinted up to a million córdobas. The dollar-linked córdoba oro ended it.

## Key figures

| figure | value | source |
|---|---|---|
| Hyperinflation (≥ 50%/month) | Jun 1986 – Mar 1991 | H&K |
| Peak month | March 1991 | H&K |
| Peak monthly inflation | 261 % | H&K |
| Doubling time at peak | 16.4 days | H&K |
| Redenomination | 14 Feb 1988 ("Operación Berta"), 1 córdoba nuevo = 1,000 córdobas | Wikipedia (Nicaraguan córdoba) |
| Largest overprints | up to 1,000,000 córdobas (on the 1,000) | Wikipedia (Nicaraguan córdoba) |

## Causes

- **The US embargo** (from 1985) cut trade and credit.
- **Central-bank financing** of the deficit and of subsidised state enterprises; price controls
  that emptied the shops.

## Timeline

- **Jun 1986** — monthly inflation passes 50 % (H&K start).
- **14 Feb 1988** — Operación Berta: córdoba nuevo at 1,000 : 1.
- **1988–1990** — notes overprinted from 10,000 up to 1,000,000 córdobas.
- **1990** — the córdoba oro is introduced at par with the dollar.
- **Mar 1991** — peak 261 % (H&K) during the conversion; the episode ends.

## Lessons

- Overprinting old notes with bigger numbers is the cheapest sign a state is printing faster than it
  can design notes.
